questions.question: Cyclohexene has an enthalpy change of hydrogenation of -120 kJ mol-1. Approximately what is the enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene? A -150, B -210, C -360, D -510 (kJ mol-1).
questions.answer: B -210 kJ mol-1
steps: Three C=C bonds in a localised Kekule structure would give 3 x (-120) = -360 kJ mol-1.
Benzene is actually more stable than this, because its delocalised ring of electrons lowers its energy.
Its hydrogenation is therefore less exothermic than -360 kJ mol-1, by about the delocalisation energy (about 150 kJ mol-1).
-360 + 150 = -210 kJ mol-1, so option B is the closest value.

Sulfuric acid is not oxidised by dichromate, so it is the best choice.

questions.question: A 1.53 g steel wire was dissolved and made up to 250.0 cm3. 25.0 cm3 portions were titrated with 0.0195 mol dm-3 KMnO4; the mean titre was 27.35 cm3. Calculate the percentage of iron in the wire to 3 significant figures.
steps: Overall ionic equation: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O, so 5 mol Fe2+ react with 1 mol MnO4-.
The whole 250.0 cm3 is 10 times larger, so n(Fe) = 2.667 x 10^-2 mol.

questions.question: A student made up the iron(II) solution with distilled water instead of dilute sulfuric acid, and a brown suspension formed during titration. Explain how, if at all, the titre would be affected.
questions.answer: The titre is larger (too high), because in neutral solution MnO4- is reduced only to brown MnO2 (3 electrons) rather than Mn2+ (5 electrons), so more MnO4- is needed per Fe2+
steps: In acid, MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O, so each MnO4- takes 5 electrons.
Without acid, MnO4- is reduced only to brown MnO2: MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-, which takes 3 electrons.
Each Fe2+ supplies only 1 electron, so more MnO4- (1/3 mol per Fe2+ instead of 1/5 mol) is needed.
Hence a larger titre is recorded than the true value.
The brown solid also makes the end-point harder to see.
The calculated iron content would therefore be too high.

Sn2+ is reduced to Sn and forms the right-hand (positive) electrode, written as Sn2+(aq)|Sn(s).

questions.question: E(Fe/Fe2+) = -0.44 V and the cell emf for Fe(s) + Sn2+(aq) -> Fe2+(aq) + Sn(s) is +0.30 V. What is E(Sn/Sn2+)? A -0.74 V, B -0.14 V, C +0.14 V, D +0.74 V.
steps: E(cell) = E(right-hand electrode) - E(left-hand electrode), with both as reduction potentials.
The right-hand electrode is Sn2+/Sn and the left-hand is Fe2+/Fe, with E(Fe2+/Fe) = -0.44 V.

questions.question: The standard hydrogen electrode uses platinum coated with platinum black. What is the purpose of this coating? A to increase the rate of the equilibrium between hydrogen gas and hydrogen ions, B to provide an inert protective coating, C to increase electrical conductivity, D to ensure the conditions remain standard.
questions.answer: A to increase the rate of the equilibrium between hydrogen gas and hydrogen ions
steps: Platinum black is finely divided platinum, which has a very large surface area.
The large surface area lets H2 gas and H+ ions reach equilibrium quickly at the electrode surface.
It does not act as a protective coating, change conductivity significantly, or control conditions.
So option A is correct.

questions.question: What is the reaction at the anode in an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell? A O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-, B 4OH- -> O2 + 2H2O + 4e-, C 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-, D H2 + 2OH- -> 2H2O + 2e-.
steps: The anode is the negative electrode, where oxidation takes place.
Hydrogen is oxidised: H2 loses electrons (oxidation number 0 to +1).
In alkaline conditions the hydroxide ions supply the O atoms: H2 + 2OH- -> 2H2O + 2e-.
Option D is the only oxidation half-equation for hydrogen.

questions.question: Which is true of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell? A the cathode has a more positive potential than the anode, B hydrogen is oxidised at the cathode, C oxygen is reduced at the negative electrode, D the cell potential is different under alkaline or acidic conditions.
questions.answer: A the cathode has a more positive potential than the anode
steps: The cathode is the positive electrode, where reduction occurs (oxygen is reduced).
The anode is the negative electrode, where hydrogen is oxidised.
So the cathode is more positive than the anode, making A true.
B and C are wrong, since hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode.
D is wrong, because the standard cell potential is 1.23 V under both alkaline and acidic conditions.

questions.question: Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells have advantages over methanol-oxygen fuel cells in vehicles. Which is an advantage? A more energy is released per mole of fuel, B emissions do not contribute to climate change, C hydrogen is easier to store than methanol, D only hydrogen can be obtained from renewable resources.
questions.answer: B emissions do not contribute to climate change
steps: The hydrogen fuel cell produces only water as its product: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
Methanol fuel cells produce carbon dioxide, which is a greenhouse gas.

questions.answer: AsH3(g) -> As(s) + 3H+(aq) + 3e-
steps: Arsenic in AsH3 is -3 and in arsenic metal it is 0, so 3 electrons are lost per As.

questions.question: 350 cm3 of arsine at 115 000 Pa and 20 C reacts with 488 cm3 of 0.102 mol dm-3 cerium(IV) sulfate, forming arsenic. Calculate the final oxidation state of the cerium ion.
questions.answer: +3 (Ce4+ is reduced to Ce3+)
steps: Each AsH3 loses 3 electrons, so electrons lost = 3 x 0.0165 = 0.0496 mol.
Electrons gained per Ce = 0.0496 / 0.0498 = 1.00, so each Ce gains one electron.
Ce4+ + e- -> Ce3+, so the final oxidation state of cerium is +3.

questions.question: The redox reaction 2V2+(aq) + Cu2+(aq) -> 2V3+(aq) + Cu(s) is carried out in a cell. What is the cell diagram? questions.answer: D Pt(s) | V2+(aq), V3+(aq) || Cu2+(aq) | Cu(s)
steps: V2+ is oxidised to V3+ and Cu2+ is reduced to Cu.
V2+ and V3+ are both in solution, so the left electrode must be inert (Pt), not vanadium metal.

questions.question: Zinc electrode increased in mass by 1.635 g while electrode G decreased in mass by 0.6075 g during current flow. Metal G is: A copper, B iron, C magnesium, D manganese.
questions.answer: C magnesium
steps: Zn2+ + 2e- -> Zn, so electrons passed = 2 x (1.635 / 65.38) = 0.0500 mol.
The same charge dissolves G as G2+: G -> G2+ + 2e-, so moles of G = 0.0500 / 2 = 0.0250 mol.
Molar mass of G = 0.6075 / 0.0250 = 24.3 g mol-1.
This matches magnesium (24.3 g mol-1), so the answer is C.

questions.question: What is the minimum volume of oxygen needed for complete combustion of a mixture of 50 cm3 propene and 50 cm3 but-1-ene, with all volumes at the same temperature and pressure? A 225, B 300, C 525, D 700 (cm3).
questions.answer: C 525 cm3
steps: Propene: C3H6 + 4.5O2 -> 3CO2 + 3H2O, so 50 cm3 needs 50 x 4.5 = 225 cm3 O2.
But-1-ene: C4H8 + 6O2 -> 4CO2 + 4H2O, so 50 cm3 needs 50 x 6 = 300 cm3 O2.
Equal conditions mean volume ratios equal mole ratios (Avogadro).
Total oxygen = 225 + 300 = 525 cm3, option C.

questions.question: For 4V3+(aq) + O2(g) + 2H2O(l) -> 4VO2+(aq) + 4H+(aq), which statement can be deduced from this information alone? A the reaction will not occur under any conditions, B reactants are kinetically stable, C reactants are thermodynamically unstable with respect to products, D aqueous V3+ oxidises rapidly on standing in air.
questions.answer: C the reactants are thermodynamically unstable with respect to the products
steps: A feasibility (thermodynamic) statement can only be made from the equation, which is shown to be feasible in one direction.
The equation alone does not show the rate, so statements about kinetics (B and D) cannot be deduced.
Statement A claims no conditions allow reaction, which cannot be deduced from one equation.
Only statement C, thermodynamic instability of the reactants, is deducible from the feasibility of the reaction.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of the apparatus to measure the standard electrode potential of a Cu2+(aq)|Cu(s) electrode against a standard hydrogen electrode, including the essential conditions.
questions.answer: Cu electrode in 1.00 mol dm-3 Cu2+(aq) joined by a salt bridge and voltmeter to an SHE (Pt black in 1.00 mol dm-3 H+ with H2 at 100 kPa), at 298 K
steps: SHE: platinum electrode coated with platinum black, dipped in 1.00 mol dm-3 H+(aq) (e.g. HCl), with H2 gas at 100 kPa (1.00 x 10^5 Pa) bubbled over it.
Second half-cell: copper electrode in 1.00 mol dm-3 Cu2+(aq) (e.g. CuSO4(aq)).
Essential conditions: 298 K (25 C), 1.00 mol dm-3 solutions and 100 kPa for the gas.

Connect both electrodes to a high-resistance voltmeter; the Cu electrode is the positive terminal, and the reading is E(Cu2+/Cu).

questions.question: Given E(Cr2O7 2-/Cr3+) = +1.33 V and E(Cl2/Cl-) = +1.36 V, explain in terms of electrode potentials why acidified dichromate(VI) ions react with concentrated hydrochloric acid to form chlorine, even though E(cell) = -0.03 V.
questions.answer: E(cell) = -0.03 V applies only under standard conditions (1 mol dm-3). Concentrated HCl has high [H+], which makes E(Cr2O7 2-/Cr3+) more positive, and high [Cl-], which makes E(Cl2/Cl-) less positive, so E(cell) becomes positive and the reaction is feasible
steps: Under standard conditions E(cell) = +1.33 - 1.36 = -0.03 V, so the reaction is not feasible at 1 mol dm-3.
Concentrated HCl means non-standard conditions: [H+] and [Cl-] are much greater than 1 mol dm-3.
High [H+] shifts Cr2O7 2- + 14H+ + 6e- <=> 2Cr3+ + 7H2O to the right, so E(Cr2O7 2-/Cr3+) becomes more positive.
High [Cl-] shifts Cl2 + 2e- <=> 2Cl- to the left, so E(Cl2/Cl-) becomes less positive.
E(cell) therefore becomes positive, so dichromate(VI) oxidises Cl- to Cl2.

questions.question: Write the cell diagram, using the conventional representation of half-cells, for the reaction that produces chlorine from dichromate(VI) ions and chloride ions.
questions.answer: Pt(s) | Cl-(aq) | Cl2(g) || Cr2O7 2-(aq), H+(aq), Cr3+(aq) | Pt(s)
steps: Chloride is oxidised to chlorine at the anode (left), so it is written as Pt(s) | Cl-(aq) | Cl2(g).
Dichromate is reduced at the cathode (right) and is written as Cr2O7 2-(aq), H+(aq), Cr3+(aq) | Pt(s).
Oxidised and reduced forms are shown in each half-cell, with the inert Pt electrodes at each end.
The two half-cells are joined by a double line ||.

questions.question: 25.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol dm-3 X2O5 is reduced by a reducing agent. The reduced product is then oxidised back to its original state using 50.0 cm3 of 0.0200 mol dm-3 acidified MnO4-. Calculate the oxidation state of X after reduction.

questions.question: The positive electrode reaction in an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell is O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-. What is the negative electrode half-equation? A H2 + 2OH- -> 2H2O + 2e-, B H2 + OH- -> H2O + H+ + 2e-, C H2 -> 2H+ + 2e-, D H2 + H2O -> 3H+ + OH- + 2e-.

questions.question: Which reaction is thermodynamically feasible? A 2Ce + 3Mg2+ -> 2Ce3+ + 3Mg, B 4Ce3+ -> Ce + 3Ce4+, C 3Mn2+ -> Mn + 2Mn3+, D Mg + 2Ce4+ -> Mg2+ + 2Ce3+.
questions.answer: D Mg + 2Ce4+ -> Mg2+ + 2Ce3+
steps: A reaction is feasible when E(cell) = E(reduction) - E(oxidation) is positive.
Mg is a strong reductant (Mg2+/Mg is about -2.37 V) and Ce4+/Ce3+ is strongly oxidising (about +1.6 V).
E(cell) for D is about +1.6 - (-2.37) = +3.9 V, which is strongly feasible.
Option A is not feasible because Mg2+ is harder to reduce than Ce3+ is, and option B and C are disproportionations that are not feasible for these ions.
So option D is the feasible reaction.

questions.question: Air contains 405 ppm of carbon dioxide. What is the approximate volume of carbon dioxide in 250 cm3 of this air? A 0.001, B 0.01, C 0.1, D 1 (cm3).
questions.answer: C 0.1 cm3
steps: 1 ppm means 1 cm3 of gas per 10^6 cm3 of air.
Volume of CO2 = 405 x 10^-6 x 250 = 0.101 cm3.
The approximate value is 0.1 cm3, option C.

questions.question: A titre has an uncertainty of 0.32 %. Each burette reading has an uncertainty of +/-0.05 cm3. What is the most likely value of the titre? A 6.40, B 15.60, C 31.25, D 32.00 (cm3).
steps: A titre is the difference of two burette readings, so its uncertainty is 2 x 0.05 = 0.10 cm3.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.10 / titre x 100 = 0.32 %.

questions.question: A hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell has an alkaline electrolyte, and the anode half-equation is H2 + 2OH- -> 2H2O + 2e-. What is the cathode half-equation? A 1/2O2 + H2O + 2e- -> 2OH-, B O2 + 2H+ + 2e- -> H2O2, C 1/2O2 + 2H+ + 2e- -> H2O, D O2 + H2 + 2e- -> 2OH-.
steps: The cathode is where oxygen is reduced.
In alkaline conditions the reduction product is OH-, and water supplies the H atoms.
Option A gives 2OH- from 1/2 O2, H2O and 2 electrons, which balances in O, H and charge.
Options B and C use H+ ions, which are not present in alkaline solution.

questions.question: Why is no indicator necessary in the redox titration of iron(II) ions with potassium manganate(VII)? A an indicator would interfere with the redox reaction, B no suitable indicator changes colour, C the colour change of iron(II) is sufficient, D the colour change of manganate(VII) is sufficient.
questions.answer: D the colour change of the manganate(VII) ions is sufficient
steps: MnO4- is intensely purple and is reduced to very pale Mn2+ during the titration.
The first permanent pale pink colour shows that all the Fe2+ has been oxidised.
So the manganate(VII) acts as its own indicator, and option D is correct.

questions.question: State the conditions, in addition to 1 mol dm-3 solutions, required for standard electrode potentials.

steps: Standard electrode potentials are measured at a fixed temperature of 298 K.
Any gas involved, such as H2 in the SHE, is at a pressure of 100 kPa.

questions.question: Calculate the standard electrode potential of a Daniell cell made from Zn2+/Zn and Cu2+/Cu standard electrodes. Standard values (vs SHE): Cu2+/Cu = +0.34 V, Zn2+/Zn = -0.76 V.
steps: Copper is reduced (right-hand, positive) and zinc is oxidised (left-hand, negative).
E(cell) = +1.10 V.

questions.question: Give three observations that would be made when current flows for several hours in the Daniell cell.
questions.answer: Zinc electrode dissolves (gets smaller); copper deposits on the copper electrode (gets larger); the blue Cu2+(aq) colour fades
steps: Zn is oxidised at the negative electrode: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-, so the zinc electrode dissolves and loses mass.
Cu2+ is reduced at the positive electrode: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu, so pink-brown copper is deposited and the copper electrode gains mass.
The concentration of Cu2+(aq) falls, so the blue colour of the copper(II) sulfate solution fades.
The question asks for three observations, so give all three.

questions.question: State and justify, in terms of E(cell) values, whether copper(I) ions and iron(II) ions will disproportionate. Include any equations.
questions.answer: Cu+ will disproportionate (E(cell) = +0.36 V); Fe2+ will not (E(cell) = -1.21 V)
steps: Cu+ disproportionation: 2Cu+ -> Cu2+ + Cu, using E(Cu+/Cu) = +0.52 V and E(Cu2+/Cu+) = +0.16 V (Data Booklet).
E(cell) = E(reduction) - E(oxidation) = +0.52 - 0.16 = +0.36 V, which is positive, so Cu+ disproportionates.
Fe2+ disproportionation: 2Fe2+ -> Fe + Fe3+ would use E(Fe2+/Fe) = -0.44 V and E(Fe3+/Fe2+) = +0.77 V.
E(cell) = -0.44 - 0.77 = -1.21 V, which is negative, so Fe2+ does not disproportionate.

questions.question: State one reason why feasibility determined from standard electrode potentials does not necessarily mean that a reaction occurs.
questions.answer: The reaction may be kinetically slow because it has a high activation energy
steps: E(cell) shows whether a reaction is thermodynamically feasible, not how fast it proceeds.
A large activation energy means the reaction can be too slow to observe.
Non-standard conditions can also change the outcome, but activation energy is the key reason.

questions.question: An iron(II) solution contains Fe2+. 25.0 cm3 was diluted to 100.0 cm3, and 25.0 cm3 portions of the diluted solution were titrated with 0.0125 mol dm-3 KMnO4 (mean titre 16.20 cm3). What volume of the iron solution gives a 90.0 mg dose of iron?
steps: n(Fe2+) in a 25.0 cm3 diluted portion = 5 x 2.025 x 10^-4 = 1.0125 x 10^-3 mol.
Original [Fe2+] = 0.0405 x 4 = 0.162 mol dm-3 (25.0 cm3 diluted to 100.0 cm3).
Mass of Fe per cm3 = 0.162 x 55.85 = 9.05 mg cm-3.
Volume for 90.0 mg = 90.0 / 9.05 = 9.95 cm3 (3 significant figures).

questions.question: Explain, using electrode potentials, why concentrated hydrochloric acid should not be used to acidify potassium dichromate(VI) in place of sulfuric acid.
questions.answer: Dichromate(VI) oxidises Cl- to Cl2 (toxic gas, wrong product), so it is consumed by HCl; sulfate ions are not oxidised, so H2SO4 is used
steps: E(Cr2O7 2-/Cr3+) = +1.33 V and E(Cl2/Cl-) = +1.36 V (Data Booklet).
Under standard conditions the cell potential is -0.03 V, but in concentrated HCl the high [Cl-] makes E(Cl2/Cl-) less positive, so E(cell) becomes positive.
So dichromate oxidises chloride ions to chlorine, which is toxic and wastes the oxidising agent.
Sulfuric acid is not oxidised by dichromate, so it is the suitable acid.

questions.question: In a direct methanol fuel cell, methanol reacts with water at one electrode to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions. Write the oxidation half-equation (state symbols not required).
questions.answer: CH3OH + H2O -> CO2 + 6H+ + 6e-
steps: Methanol is oxidised: carbon goes from -2 in CH3OH to +4 in CO2, a loss of 6 electrons.
Carbon: 1 on each side. Hydrogen: 4 + 2 = 6 on the left, and 6 H+ on the right.
Oxygen: 1 + 1 = 2 on the left, 2 in CO2 on the right.
Charge: 0 on the left, and +6 - 6 = 0 on the right.

questions.question: Write the overall equation for the direct methanol fuel cell (state symbols not required).
questions.answer: 2CH3OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 4H2O
steps: Anode: CH3OH + H2O -> CO2 + 6H+ + 6e- (multiply by 2).
Cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O (multiply by 3, so 12 electrons).
Adding and cancelling 12 H+ and 2 H2O gives 2CH3OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 4H2O.
Check: 2 C, 8 H and 6 O on each side.

questions.question: Given alkaline half-equations 2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH- (E = -0.83 V) and 1/2O2 + H2O + 2e- -> 2OH- (E = +0.40 V), what is the overall cell reaction? A 3H2O + 1/2O2 -> H2 + 4OH-, B H2 + 4OH- -> 3H2O + 1/2O2, C H2 + 1/2O2 -> H2O, D H2O -> H2 + 1/2O2.
steps: The fuel cell reaction is the reduction of O2 plus the oxidation of H2.
Oxidation of H2: H2 + 2OH- -> 2H2O + 2e-, the reverse of the first half-equation.
Adding the reduction 1/2O2 + H2O + 2e- -> 2OH- gives H2 + 1/2O2 -> H2O.
The overall equation is option C, which balances with the hydroxide ions cancelled.

questions.question: State the colour change at the end-point when potassium manganate(VII), with excess sulfuric acid, is titrated with sodium ethanedioate solution.
questions.answer: From purple (pink) to colourless
steps: MnO4- is purple and acts as its own indicator.
The oxalate reduces the MnO4- to the colourless Mn2+ ion.
At the end-point all the MnO4- is used up, so the purple colour disappears and the solution is colourless.

questions.topic: Effect of Neutral Conditions on Titre
questions.question: A second titration without sulfuric acid gave a brown suspension. Explain how, if at all, the mean titre would be affected by the reaction forming this suspension (no E(cell) calculation needed).
questions.answer: The titre would be lower, because in neutral conditions MnO4- is reduced only to MnO2 (3 electrons) rather than Mn2+ (5 electrons), so less oxalate is needed per MnO4-
steps: Without acid, MnO4- is reduced to brown MnO2: MnO4- + 2H2O + 3e- -> MnO2 + 4OH-.
In acid, MnO4- is reduced to Mn2+ using 5 electrons per MnO4-.
The oxalate is oxidised to CO2 giving 2 electrons per C2O4 2-, so less oxalate is needed per MnO4- in neutral solution (3/2 instead of 5/2 mol).
The volume of oxalate titre is therefore smaller.
A smaller titre would give an underestimated MnO4- concentration.

questions.question: 5.00 g of sodium thiosulfate is weighed and made up to 250.0 cm3 in a flask of uncertainty +/-0.25 cm3. Assuming two weighings, what is the minimum balance uncertainty needed to match the flask? A +/-0.0025 g, B +/-0.005 g, C +/-0.01 g, D +/-0.05 g.
steps: Relative uncertainty of the flask = 0.25 / 250.0 = 0.10 %.
Relative uncertainty in mass should also be 0.10 %, so absolute uncertainty = 0.0010 x 5.00 g = 0.0050 g.
Two weighings each have uncertainty u, so the total = 2u = 0.0050 g.
u = 0.0025 g, option A.

questions.question: Sodium thiosulfate is in the burette, starch is added just before the end-point, and the iodine is in the conical flask. What is the colour of the solution at the end-point? A blue-black, B brown, C colourless, D yellow.
questions.answer: C colourless
steps: Iodine with starch gives a blue-black colour in the flask.
Thiosulfate reduces the iodine to colourless iodide, so the blue-black colour disappears.
At the end-point all the iodine has reacted, so the solution is colourless.

questions.question: The emf of a cell made from copper and magnesium half-cells is measured under standard conditions. The voltmeter has an uncertainty of 0.50 %. What is the highest emf that could be measured? A 2.70 V, B 2.72 V, C 2.74 V, D 2.85 V.
steps: E(cell) = E(Cu2+/Cu) - E(Mg2+/Mg) = +0.34 - (-2.37) = +2.71 V (Data Booklet).
Uncertainty = 0.50 % of 2.71 V = 0.0136 V.
Highest emf = 2.71 + 0.0136 = 2.724 V, which rounds to 2.72 V.

questions.question: For the reaction where E(cell) is positive, what can be deduced about delta Stotal and ln K? A both positive, B both negative, C delta Stotal positive and ln K negative, D delta Stotal negative and ln K positive.

steps: A positive E(cell) means delta G = -nFE(cell) is negative, so the reaction is feasible.
A negative delta G corresponds to K > 1, so ln K is positive.
delta Stotal = -delta G / T is positive when delta G is negative.
So option A is correct.

questions.question: State why a salt bridge is used rather than a wire to complete the circuit of the electrochemical cell.
questions.answer: It allows ions to flow between the half-cells, completing the circuit and keeping electrical neutrality, while keeping the two solutions separate
steps: A wire carries only electrons, so it cannot complete the ionic part of the circuit.
The salt bridge allows ions to move, keeping each half-cell electrically neutral.
It also stops the two solutions mixing, so the reactants stay separate.

questions.question: Write an equation for the reaction that takes place if current is allowed to flow through the cell (state symbols not required). The standard cell potential is +1.53 V, with a zinc half-cell.
questions.answer: Zn + 2Fe3+ -> Zn2+ + 2Fe2+
steps: Zinc is the reductant (E(Zn2+/Zn) = -0.76 V), so it is oxidised to Zn2+.
A cell potential of +1.53 V with zinc requires the other half-cell to be at +0.77 V, which is Fe3+/Fe2+.
Overall: Zn + 2Fe3+ -> Zn2+ + 2Fe2+.

questions.topic: Effect of Dilution on Cell Potential
questions.question: The standard emf of the cell is +1.53 V. State what happens to this value, if anything, when the Zn2+ solution is diluted, and justify your answer.
questions.answer: The emf increases (becomes more positive), because diluting Zn2+ (a product) lowers the reaction quotient Q, which shifts the Nernst value so E(cell) rises
steps: Using the Nernst equation, E = E-standard - (RT/nF) ln Q.
Diluting Zn2+ lowers [Zn2+] and therefore Q.
A lower Q gives a less negative ln Q term, so E(cell) increases above +1.53 V.

questions.question: Which reaction occurs at an electrode in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell? A O2 + 2H2 -> 2H2O, B O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-, C 4H+ + 4OH- -> 4H2O, D H2O + 2OH- -> 2H2 + 1/2O2 + 2e-.
steps: Option A is the overall cell reaction, not an electrode reaction.
Option C is neutralisation, which is not an electrode reaction.
Option D is the reverse of the cell reaction at the electrodes, and it is an electrolysis-type oxidation reaction, not the fuel cell reaction.
Option B is the reduction of oxygen at the positive electrode in alkaline conditions, so it is correct.
